extraction.name: The LAMBADA dataset
extraction.description: LAMBADA is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. To succeed on LAMBADA, computational models cannot simply rely on local context, but must be able to keep track of information in the broader discourse.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA consists of passages composed of a context (on average 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence. The context size is the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens (this size was chosen in a pilot study). The task is to guess the last word of the target sentence (the target word). The constraint that the target word be the last word of the sentence, while not necessary for our research goal, makes the task more natural for human subjects. The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. We randomly divided the novels into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. We built the LAMBADA dataset from the latter, with the idea that models tackling LAMBADA should be trained on raw text from the training partition, composed of 2662 novels and encompassing more than 200M words. To reduce time and cost of dataset collection, we filtered out passages that are relatively easy for standard language models, since such cases are likely to be guessable based on local context alone. A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The Book Corpus was subjected to duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered out if their target word had a probability ≥0.00175 according to any of four language models (a pre-trained recurrent neural network, a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The Book Corpus was subjected to duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Passages were filtered out if their target word had a probability ≥0.00175 according to any of four language models (a pre-trained recurrent neural network, a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects evaluated a random sample of passages through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: 1. One human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage (context and target sentence). 2. If the first guess was right, a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage. 3. If the second guess was also right, more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10. If no subject was able to guess the target word from the target sentence alone, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset. Subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence. It was ensured that the same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: two consecutive subjects were required to exactly match the missing word based on the broad context, and no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses. A strict hit-or-miss approach was used, keeping only items that could be unambiguously determined by human subjects, due to the practical and methodological challenges of determining plausible or synonymous continuations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 (for broad context) to 10 (for local context) human subjects per item.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011), a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model (used for filtering passages).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, is available for download. The test set will be made available at the time of a public competition.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text and stimulate the computational community to develop novel language models that genuinely capture non-local phenomena.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA (48%), while other categories like common nouns (37%), verbs (7.7%), adjectives, and adverbs are under-represented compared to the POS distribution in the input data. This bias towards proper names was noted as exploitable by a baseline model.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation performed is preliminary and serves as a proof-of-concept. Minor modifications to tested models are unlikely to lead to human-level performance. Standard language models are inherently bound to fail on LAMBADA by design due to the filtering process. Tracking event-related phenomena (e.g., script-like sequences of events) appears harder for subjects than co-referential phenomena in this task. The strict 'perfect-match' annotation approach might exclude passages with plausible synonymous continuations, which was a practical and financial limitation.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing, Validation (development set), and Fine Tuning of computational models for text understanding, specifically for evaluating their ability to take broad discourse context into account in a word prediction task.
